name: Francis Schaeffer
role: American Presbyterian pastor, apologist, and founder of L'Abri in Switzerland

died.cause: Lymphoma (cancer), diagnosed in 1978 and treated at the Mayo Clinic

summary: A Presbyterian pastor who, with his wife Edith, opened their Swiss chalet as L'Abri ('the shelter'), where thousands of young people came with questions about faith, art, and philosophy. His books, such as The God Who Is There and How Should We Then Live?, made him one of the most influential evangelical thinkers of the 20th century. In his last years he helped mobilize American evangelicals against abortion and called for civil disobedience against laws he considered tyrannical, shaping the rise of the Christian Right. His son Frank later wrote a critical memoir of him and the movement.

key_dates.label: Converted as a teenager after reading the Bible for himself

Becomes the first minister ordained in the Bible Presbyterian Church; pastors in Grove City, Chester, and St. Louis
Moves to Switzerland as a missionary of the Independent Board for Presbyterian Foreign Missions
Spiritual crisis in which he reexamines his faith, later described in True Spirituality
Ordered to leave the canton of Valais; founds L'Abri in Huémoz, Vaud
Publishes The God Who Is There and Escape from Reason
Book and film series How Should We Then Live?
Publishes A Christian Manifesto, urging civil disobedience against laws he saw as defying God

accomplishments.text: Founded L'Abri with Edith Schaeffer in 1955, an open home and study centre in the Swiss Alps that welcomed students and seekers of any background; branches later opened in England, the Netherlands, the United States, and elsewhere.

Developed a 'presuppositional' cultural apologetic arguing that Western thought, art, and culture had lost a basis for truth and meaning without the God of the Bible, in The God Who Is There (1968), Escape from Reason (1968), and He Is There and He Is Not Silent (1972).
Brought evangelicals into serious engagement with art, film, philosophy, and history; How Should We Then Live? (1976) was a widely viewed book and film series.
With C. Everett Koop produced Whatever Happened to the Human Race? (1979), a book and film that helped turn many American evangelicals against abortion and euthanasia.

In A Christian Manifesto (1981) urged Christians to resist the 'humanist' state through politics, the courts, and civil disobedience, and argued that force could be justified as a last resort against a tyrannical government; the book influenced the Christian Right and later anti-abortion activists, including some who blockaded clinics.
Called for a 'balanced' separatism after leaving Carl McIntire's Bible Presbyterian Church in the 1950s split, and wrote The Mark of the Christian (1970) on love as the sign of true Christians.
Warned in The Great Evangelical Disaster (1984) that evangelicals were accommodating to the culture, especially on biblical inerrancy.

His son Frank Schaeffer, after first working with him on the films, later left evangelicalism and in Crazy for God (2007) described his father as prone to rages and alleged that he sometimes hit Edith; other family members and L'Abri colleagues disputed parts of the account.

original.reference: Schaeffer's summary of L'Abri's approach, used in his books and by L'Abri
Title of his 1976 book and film, taken from Ezekiel 33:10 (KJV)
original.note: The phrase is biblical; Schaeffer made it the title of his best-known work.

persecuted_others_note: No record of Schaeffer ordering or carrying out persecution. In his last years he called for laws against abortion and for civil disobedience, and argued that force could be legitimate against a tyrannical state; critics, including his son Frank, have said this rhetoric helped inspire militant anti-abortion activism, though Schaeffer did not call for attacks on people.
persecution_note: In 1955 the authorities of the Catholic canton of Valais ordered the Schaeffers to leave because of their 'religious influence' after a local woman joined their Bible studies. They moved to Huémoz in Protestant Vaud and stayed in Switzerland. He also faced criticism and isolation within Carl McIntire's separatist movement, which split in 1956.

persecution.title: Expulsion order from the canton of Valais
persecution.summary: While the family lived at Champéry, a Catholic village in the canton of Valais, they received official letters ordering them to leave the canton for having had a 'religious influence' in the village, after a local woman began attending their Bible studies. Edith Schaeffer's account says Catholic local leaders and officials pressed for the order. The family found a chalet at Huémoz in the Protestant canton of Vaud, where they were allowed to stay, and opened L'Abri there.

responsible.name: Cantonal authorities of Valais
responsible.role: Issued the order to leave the canton

responsible.name: Local Catholic leaders in Champéry
responsible.role: Reported to have complained about their influence

persecution.outcome: The family moved to Huémoz, Vaud, and founded L'Abri; they were not expelled from Switzerland.

excommunication_note: Schaeffer was never excommunicated or deposed. He left Carl McIntire's Bible Presbyterian Church with the majority in the 1956 split; his denomination later became the Reformed Presbyterian Church, Evangelical Synod, which joined the Presbyterian Church in America in 1982.
